tldr: A new training recipe uses policy gradients through a differentiable world model to train motion tracking on a 700-muscle whole-body musculoskeletal model in just 6.3 minutes on a single RTX 5090—a 37x speedup over previous methods.
hero_caption: Prediction accuracy of the learned world model. Over the 16 steps (0.32 seconds) used for policy updates, the open-loop body position error is 7.0 mm, less than half the policy's own tracking error (18.2 mm). The rank correlation (Spearman) of cumulative return with the ground-truth simulation reaches an exceptionally high 0.995.
overview:
Musculoskeletal models simulate human motion using skeletal muscles. They are essential across biomechanics, assistive device design, and realistic character animation. However, coordinating hundreds of muscle actuators pulling on bones through tendons while making contact with the ground is notoriously difficult. With conventional model-free reinforcement learning like PPO, learning even a single motion takes hours to days on a GPU, making hyperparameter tuning painfully slow.

To tackle this, the authors looked at differentiable world models (such as SuperMimic), which dramatically sped up RL for rigid-body humanoids. These methods model environmental dynamics with neural networks and update policies directly via backpropagation through time (BPTT). However, directly applying settings tuned for rigid-body robots to a 700-muscle human body model causes training to fail almost immediately due to muscle-specific dynamics.

In this study, the authors identified the failure modes one by one and introduced four muscle-specific improvements: removing computationally expensive muscle geometry features from observations, collecting data concurrently using CUDA Graphs, using Beta exploration noise to keep excitations strictly bounded, and downsampling the control frequency to 50 Hz. As a result, MS-Human-700 reaches the tracking performance of the 3.9-hour baseline in just 6.3 minutes, achieving roughly a 37x speedup.

Furthermore, by using test-time action refinement—optimizing actions for a few gradient ascent steps through the world model at test time—they reduced tracking errors on held-out motion clips by an additional 26% with zero failures.
contributions: Built a tracking framework for 700-muscle (MS-Human-700) and 354-muscle (MyoFullBody) whole-body models using differentiable world models with MuJoCo's activation dynamics built in.

Identified why rigid-body speedup techniques fail on muscle models, and achieved a 37x speedup (reducing training from 3.9 hours to 6.3 minutes) through Beta exploration noise, concurrent data collection, and other engineering choices.
Achieved higher joint-angle tracking accuracy and fewer failures in just 20 minutes of training than prior work achieved after 3 days of PPO training.
Demonstrated that test-time action refinement through the world model eliminates failures on held-out clips and substantially cuts tracking errors.

sections.heading: The musculoskeletal control bottleneck: shrinking days of training into minutes
sections.summary: Controlling a 700-muscle whole-body model is exceptionally challenging due to over-actuation, complex tendon routing, and non-linear activation dynamics. While conventional RL took days of compute, this work proposes a recipe using differentiable world models that trains tracking policies in minutes.
sections.details:
Musculoskeletal models of the human body sit at an exciting intersection of motor control, biomechanics, and embodied AI. Whole-body models like MS-Human-700 (700 muscles) and MyoFullBody (354 muscles) feature Hill-type muscles pulling tendons wrapped around bones, massive joint redundancy (over-actuation), and no direct torque control. Faithfully tracking motion-capture clips on unseen data while managing contacts is remarkably hard.

Standard model-free reinforcement learning (such as PPO) requires massive compute. For instance, prior work like MuscleMimic trained policies for 3.2 billion steps, taking around three days on an H100 GPU. When a single experiment takes hours or days, tuning hyperparameters becomes prohibitively expensive.

Meanwhile, in the rigid-body humanoid community (e.g., Unitree G1), model-based methods like SuperMimic and BlinkMimic have drastically cut training times to minutes by 'imagining' rollouts inside a learned world model and backpropagating reward gradients directly. But trying to apply these speedups to musculoskeletal models fails immediately due to excitation inputs bounded in $[0,1]$, heavy muscle-tendon geometry calculations, and muscle-specific dynamics.

This paper provides the recipe to make fast world-model training work reliably on whole-body musculoskeletal models. On a single RTX 5090, it drops training time on MS-Human-700 from the 3.9-hour baseline down to 6.3 minutes, achieving lower tracking errors in 20 minutes than the baseline reaches after 10 hours.

sections.heading: Trends in musculoskeletal control and differentiable dynamics
sections.summary: Musculoskeletal control has long been dominated by model-free RL like PPO, where long training times formed a major bottleneck. This study represents the first systematic success in adapting the fast, differentiable world-model techniques developed for rigid robots to muscle models.
sections.details:
### Musculoskeletal simulation and control
Since the introduction of MyoSuite for musculoskeletal models in MuJoCo, researchers have explored dexterous manipulation and locomotion. For whole-body models like MS-Human-700 and MyoFullBody, prior efforts have explored muscle synergy dimension reduction and PPO-based motion tracking. Recently, MS-Emulator trained MS-Human-700 on a running motion using a GPU-parallel simulator, but imitating a single trajectory still took 7 hours on an RTX 5090. This work uses the same models and tracking task definitions to train a general tracking policy across all 108 unseen clips in just 20 minutes.

### Tracking control through learned dynamics
For rigid-body characters and robots, policy optimization through differentiable simulators (DiffMimic, SHAC) or learned neural world models (SuperMimic, InstantTrack, BlinkMimic) has yielded impressive results. In particular, BlinkMimic cut Unitree G1 tracking training to a few minutes. However, directly applying these fast settings to muscle models causes training to collapse. This paper systematically uncovers what works and what fails on muscles.

### Test-time action refinement
Combining policy execution with test-time planning has been explored in works like TD-MPC2 and Qflex. In this paper, test-time action refinement via gradient ascent is used as a probe to inspect how closely the policy reaches the world model's optimal solutions.

sections.heading: Why do muscles break the pipeline? Four recipes for fast training
sections.summary: The authors built a differentiable world model incorporating MuJoCo's muscle activation dynamics and fixed the settings that failed on muscle systems. Four key changes—removing muscle geometry observations, CUDA Graph concurrent collection, bounded Beta noise, and 50 Hz control—unlocked massive speedups.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Foundations of musculoskeletal models and differentiable world models
The state $x$ includes skeleton position and velocity, along with muscle activations $a \in [0,1]^M$. At each control step, the policy outputs muscle excitation commands $e \in [0,1]^M$, and activations transition according to MuJoCo's first-order differential equations. The world model $f_\phi$ solves activation dynamics $a$ analytically using the exact same discretization as the simulator (matching it to floating-point precision), while using an MLP only to predict skeletal accelerations and foot contact forces.

The policy $\pi_\theta$ performs an imagined rollout of $H$ steps inside the world model and is updated directly via BPTT (backpropagation through time) to maximize analytical tracking rewards, terminal rewards, and a bootstrapped terminal value function (Critic).

### 3.3 The Fast Recipe
Three settings borrowed from rigid G1 setups failed on the 700-muscle model:
- **Unconstrained bootstrapped values without warm-up**: The critic diverged early in training, driving imagined returns to more than 10x their theoretical maximum. The fix: a 200-iteration world-model-only pre-training phase, and clamping the value function at its theoretical upper bound.
- **An initial 4x policy learning rate**: While it pulled ahead early on, half the runs crashed irrecoverably. Because the muscle count is massive, the policy easily drifted into unvisited states. The learning rate was fixed to the standard 1x.
- **Evaluation-guided resets**: Resetting just before failure states works well on rigid models, but on 5-second clips early failures occurred across almost the entire clip. The full search overhead doubled wall-clock time, so it was disabled.

On top of these fixes, the authors introduced **four distinct improvements**:
- **(a) Removing muscle geometry from observations**: Muscle lengths, velocities, and tendon routing calculations are the heaviest part of imagination updates. Since these can be inferred from skeletal states, dropping them from observations removed them from the computational graph entirely.
- **(b) Concurrent data collection and policy updates**: The entire environment rollout was captured in a single CUDA Graph and executed on a separate stream concurrently with policy updates. Iteration time became bounded by $\max(T_{\mathrm{collect}}, T_{\mathrm{update}})$, making 1024 parallel environments more than enough.
- **(c) Beta distribution exploration noise**: Clipping standard Gaussian noise to $[0,1]$ creates a positive bias for muscles near zero excitation (relaxed state), artificially forcing unwanted tonic co-contraction. The authors used Beta distribution noise instead, whose mean strictly equals the command $e$ and whose variance naturally vanishes near the boundaries.
- **(d) 50 Hz control**: Lowering the control frequency from 100 Hz to 50 Hz (20 ms interval) halved the imagination rollout steps ($H=16$). The exploration noise variance was rescaled so its time-integrated effect remained constant.

### 3.4 Test-Time Action Refinement
Starting from the trained policy's output $e_\pi$, the world model runs a few gradient ascent steps to maximize the imagined return, executing the best candidate action in the simulator.

sections.heading: Tracking achieved in just 6.3 minutes: ablations and test-time refinement
sections.summary: On a single RTX 5090, the new recipe reached the baseline's 3.9-hour tracking performance in just 6.3 minutes (a 37x speedup). Ablations confirmed the critical role of Beta noise and control rate. Moreover, test-time action refinement eliminated all failures on unseen clips and reduced position error by an extra 26%.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Dramatic speedup in training
The baseline (SuperMimic's original design directly extended to muscle models) took 3.9 hours (2.3 seconds per iteration) to reach a normalized return of 0.83 across 108 unseen test clips. With the system optimizations in this work, iteration time dropped to 0.14 seconds. Adding Beta noise and 50 Hz control brought the time to reach 0.83 down to just 6.3 minutes (a 37x speedup). A policy trained for 20 minutes outperformed the baseline trained for 10 hours.

### 4.2 Ablation study: what is specific to muscles?
- **Learning rate**: Increasing the initial learning rate caused training to stall completely in half of the seeds. In a massive 700-dimensional action space, the policy easily outruns what the model and critic can reliably predict.
- **Exploration noise**: Performance ranked as 'Beta noise > clipped Gaussian noise > reflected Gaussian noise'. The positive bias at boundary limits corrupted world model learning; preserving relaxed muscle states via Beta distributions proved essential.

### 4.3 Tracking accuracy comparison
After 20 minutes of training, the policy achieved an 18 mm mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) and a 3.4-degree joint angle error across the 108 test clips. Compared to the official model from MuscleMimic (trained for 3 days with PPO), it had fewer failed clips and superior joint angle accuracy.

### 4.4 The impact of test-time action refinement
At test time, refining policy actions by just 5 gradient ascent steps through the world model reduced MPJPE in the actual environment by another 26%, reduced global position error by 53%, and brought the failure rate on test clips down to 0%. This demonstrates that the policy network alone does not fully tap into the predictive power of the world model.

captions.F1: Prediction error curves for the world model on unseen clips. Over the policy update horizon of 16 steps (20 ms x 16 = 0.32 s), the closed-loop error (blue) stays at just 3.1 mm, and even the open-loop error (red) is only 7.0 mm—far more accurate than the policy's own tracking error (dashed line, 18.2 mm). As shown on the right, the correlation between imagined and actual returns is exceptionally high.

sections.heading: Conclusion: bringing whole-body muscle control into the minute-scale era
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that motion tracking for a 700-muscle human body model can be learned in minutes on a single GPU. Combining accurate dynamics modeling, tailored exploration noise, and test-time refinement represents a major milestone for model-based RL in high-dimensional biomechanical control.
sections.details:
This paper proves that training whole-body motion tracking on models with 700 muscles can be compressed from days or hours down to mere minutes.

By integrating MuJoCo's activation dynamics directly into the world model and applying smart engineering—dropping tendon geometry from observations, concurrent CUDA Graph execution, bounded Beta exploration noise, and 50 Hz control—training time plunged from 3.9 hours to 6.3 minutes. In addition, the learned world model serves as an exceptionally reliable guide for test-time planning, where action refinement unlocks even higher tracking accuracy.

Turning hyperparameter tuning and experimental iterations into a matter of minutes marks a major milestone that will accelerate future research across biomechanics and embodied AI.

sections.heading: Appendix: long clips (LAFAN1), EMG discrepancies, and implementation details
sections.summary: Longer motions (LAFAN1) suffer from cumulative horizontal drift, but improving goal representations and using test-time action refinement substantially boosted completion rates. Meanwhile, the authors candidly report biomechanical limitations, such as discrepancies between generated muscle activations and biological EMG.
sections.details:
### Long clips (LAFAN1) and the drift problem
Unlike the 5-second clips from the primary KIT dataset, the multi-minute LAFAN1 motions run into 'horizontal drift': while body posture is tracked well, the pelvis (root) gradually shifts horizontally until the trajectory drifts by over 1 meter and fails. This occurred because the policy's observation lacked relative horizontal target positions.

By adding a 'relative-root goal' that supplies target position and orientation in the body frame, and pairing it with test-time action refinement ($K=5$ steps), the policy successfully completed an average of 5.5 out of 7 long clips from start to finish.

### Comparing muscle activations with biological EMG
Comparing the learned policy's muscle activation patterns with human electromyography (EMG) data during walking showed a very weak correlation of around 0.1. The prior MuscleMimic baseline showed a similar result; both models tend to rely on excessive muscle co-contraction. While adding an effort penalty to the reward reduces co-contraction, it hurts tracking accuracy. Generating biomechanically faithful muscle activity remains an open challenge.

### Why training-time action refinement fails
Attempting to distill refined actions back into the policy during training (regressing to action targets) severely degraded performance. Because the world model's gradients carry small residual modeling errors, updating the policy toward imperfect targets pushed it to collect data in regions where the model was inaccurate, creating a vicious cycle.

captions.F2: Stable whole-body tracking on an unseen, multi-minute LAFAN1 clip using the MS-Human-700 model with test-time action refinement (K=5). Muscles with higher activation levels are highlighted with darker coloring.
captions.F3: Tracking comparison on a long dance motion in MyoFullBody. The unrefined policy (orange) drifts horizontally by over 1 meter around 40 seconds and fails. With test-time action refinement (dark red), the model closely tracks the target trajectory (blue) and completes 138 seconds of motion.

takeaways: For $[0,1]$-bounded control inputs in muscle models, clipping Gaussian noise creates a positive bias (forcing unwanted co-contraction in relaxed muscles) that derails learning; mean-preserving Beta distribution noise is crucial.
In reinforcement learning with differentiable world models, omitting expensive observations like muscle-tendon geometry significantly slashes computation without hurting tracking performance.

Wrapping environment rollouts into a CUDA Graph and executing them concurrently with updates on a separate stream maximizes GPU utilization, enabling ultra-fast iterations with just 1024 parallel environments.

A policy network alone does not fully exploit the world model's predictive capacity; taking a few gradient ascent steps (action refinement) at test time dramatically boosts tracking precision and prevents failures.
limitations: Learned muscle activation patterns have a very low correlation with human electromyography (EMG) data (~0.1) and exhibit excessive co-contraction, leaving biological fidelity an open challenge.
On multi-minute motions, models tend to suffer from horizontal root drift even when posture is tracked accurately, requiring careful design of goal representations.
While test-time action refinement significantly improves tracking accuracy, it increases per-step computational cost roughly 4x, requiring further optimization for strict real-time control.
